uzSpace.title: Uzbekistan's
uzSpace.subtitle: From the ancient observatories of Samarkand to the future of satellite engineering, Uzbekistan has always looked to the stars. Join us as we build the next chapter.
uzSpace.ulughBeg: Mirzo Ulug'bek (Mīrzā Muḥammad Ṭarāghāy ibn Shāhrukh)
uzSpace.ulughBegRole: Timurid prince & astronomer; ruler of Mavarannahr (Transoxiana) from Samarkand
uzSpace.ulughBegDesc: Grandson of Amir Timur (Tamerlane), he governed Transoxiana and made Samarkand a capital of exact science. His observatory and Zij-i Sultani tied Uzbekistan’s name to global star-mapping and calendar precision.
uzSpace.ulughBegHistory:
Historical depth: Mirzo Ulug'bek (1394–1449) governed Transoxiana (Mavarannahr) as a Timurid prince-scientist. Around 1424 he founded the Samarkand Observatory on the Kuhak hill; its monumental meridian arc (about 11 metres along the rim of a sextant-scale instrument) let astronomers measure zenith distances of the Sun and stars with far smaller error than typical portable instruments. Scholars such as Ghiyath al-Din al-Kashi (until his death in 1429) and later Ali Qushji refined instruments and mathematics on site.

The observatory’s main legacy is the Zij-i Sultani (also called Zij-i Guragani)—a handbook of tables and a star catalogue listing 1,018 stars with ecliptic coordinates, together with a refined value for the obliquity of the ecliptic (~23°30'). Copies spread to Istanbul, Dehli, and Europe via Persian and Arabic manuscripts, influencing astronomical practice for centuries. Ulug'bek was killed in 1449 in a princely coup, but his data survived in manuscript tradition as a symbol of Central Asian science.
uzSpace.ulughBegPoints: Timurid statecraft + science: patronage of madrasas and observatory as one project|1424–1429: Samarkand Observatory with a large meridian instrument for fixed-site precision|Collaboration with al-Kashi on trigonometry and π for instrument design|Zij-i Sultani: 1,018 stars, solar & planetary tables used by later Muslim and Indian astronomers|Latitude of Samarkand fixed in the zij for local timekeeping and calendar reform|After 1449: observatory partly dismantled, but tables copied across Persianate world and studied in Europe
uzSpace.farghaniRole: Abū al-ʿAbbās Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad ibn Kathīr al-Farghānī — astronomer & mathematician; Ferghana Valley → Abbasid Baghdad
uzSpace.farghaniDesc: From the Ferghana region in Central Asia (today’s Uzbekistan), he distilled Ptolemaic and early Islamic astronomy into clear manuals. Latin translations shaped medieval universities and linked his work to later tables from Cairo to Samarqand.
uzSpace.farghaniHistory:
Historical depth: Abu al-Abbas Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Kathir al-Farghani (Latin: Alfraganus, d. c. 861) came from the Ferghana Valley in Central Asia and worked in Abbasid Baghdad—then the largest scientific city in the world. His Kitab fi harakat al-nujum (“Book on celestial motions,” often Latinized) gave a clear, ordered account of the Ptolemaic cosmos: epicycles, eccentrics, lunar parallax, eclipses, and a famous estimate of Earth’s diameter by comparing arc length to shadow angles.

Latin translations (12th–13th c., e.g. via translators such as John of Seville) became standard university texts alongside Sacrobosco, and parameters from this tradition echoed for centuries in geographical handbooks—one route by which Central Asian astronomy entered wider debates about measuring the Earth. Al-Farg‘oniy also wrote on the sundial, astrolabe, and armillary ring, and his star lore helped unify Arabic star names with Greek constellations for later Islamic observatories—including the intellectual line that would reach Samarkand under Ulug'bek.
uzSpace.farghaniPoints: Ferghana → Baghdad: Central Asian scholar in the heart of Abbasid science|Summarized Ptolemy for students: planets, spheres, eclipses, parallax|Earth’s size: geometric method using one degree of meridian arc|Medieval Latin “Alfraganus”: backbone of European astronomy courses before Copernicus|Instruments: sundials, astrolabes, rings—practical astronomy for mosques & navigation|Long reception: his parameters echoed in later zij tables from Cairo to Samarqand

lab.exoSubtitle: When a planet passes in front of its star, the star dims a little. Find planets the way the TESS telescope does — and see why small stars make small planets easy to spot.
lab.exoPredictQuestion: If the planet's radius doubles, how many times deeper does the dip get?
lab.exoPredictRight: Right! The dip is the share of the star's disc the planet covers, and area goes as the radius squared: 2² = 4. Check it with the radius slider.
lab.exoPredictWrong: Not quite. The dip is the share of the star's disc the planet covers, and area goes as the radius squared, so doubling the radius makes the dip 2² = 4 times deeper. Check it with the radius slider.
lab.exoNoiseWarning: This dip is smaller than the noise, so a single transit cannot show it. TESS finds planets like this by adding many transits together.
lab.exoHuntIntro: A planet orbits this star, but we cannot see it — only the star's light. Tap the dips in the light curve: the depth and the star's size give the planet's size, and the spacing gives its year. Mark at least two neighbouring transits.
lab.exoResultEmpty: Tap a dip in the light curve first.
lab.exoResultMiss: Marks not on a dip: {n}. That is noise. Tap a mark again to remove it.
lab.exoResultOne: One transit found. Mark the next one to measure the period.
lab.exoResultSkipped: There is another dip between your marks. Mark neighbouring transits.
lab.exoResultMeasured: Your measurement: radius ≈ {radius} × Earth, period {period} days.
lab.exoResultTruth: The real planet: radius {radius} × Earth, period {period} days.
lab.exoModelNote: Model: a circular orbit seen exactly edge-on (real transits that miss the star's centre are a little shorter), no limb darkening, and 400 ppm of noise every 10 minutes whatever the star (a real faint red dwarf is noisier). The star's dimming in the picture is exaggerated so it can be seen. Typical stars: rounded from Pecaut & Mamajek (2013). Real planets: Torres, Winn & Holman (2008); Bourrier et al. (2018); Agol et al. (2021). Radii: IAU 2015 Resolution B3; transit duration: Seager & Mallén-Ornelas (2003); size classes: Borucki et al. (2011).

lab.hzPredictQuestion: Around a red dwarf (M), is the habitable zone closer to the star than around the Sun, or farther?

lab.hzPredictWrong: Not quite. A red dwarf gives out about fifty times less light than the Sun, so a planet has to huddle close to it to stay warm — the zone is a few tenths of an au out. Pick the M star and find it.

lab.seasonSubtitle: Seasons come from the tilt of Earth's axis, not from the distance to the Sun.
lab.seasonFactText: Earth is closest to the Sun on {near} ({nearKm} million km) and farthest on {far} ({farKm} million km). So the Sun is nearest during our winter — distance does not make the seasons.
lab.seasonQuestion: Earth is closest to the Sun in January. So why is it winter here?
lab.seasonAnswerRight: Right! In January the northern hemisphere is tilted away from the Sun: its light arrives at a low angle and the day is short. The distance changes by only about 3%.
lab.seasonAnswerWrong: Not quite: if distance were the reason, January would be the warmest month. The northern hemisphere is tilted away from the Sun then — its light arrives low and the day is short.

Sunrise and sunset are on each city's standard time — none of these cities uses daylight saving. Noon light ignores the atmosphere. Dates are for 2026.

lab.apolloMissionCompare: Stand the rocket beside something you know
lab.apolloExplainSimple: Let go of a blown-up balloon and it shoots away: the air rushes out one way, the balloon goes the other. A rocket does the same with hot gas, thousands of times harder. And it throws its empty stages away as it climbs — like dropping empty water bottles from your backpack so you can run faster.
lab.apolloExplainFormula1: Action = reaction: the push of the gas on the rocket = the push of the rocket on the gas (Newton's third law)
lab.apolloExplainFormula2: Δv = vₑ · ln(m₀ / m₁)   (Tsiolkovsky's rocket equation)
lab.apolloExplainDetails: m₀ is the mass with fuel, m₁ the mass once that fuel is gone, vₑ the speed of the exhaust. Dropping an empty stage makes the next m₀ much smaller, so the same fuel buys far more speed — that is why the Saturn V had three stages.
lab.apolloFactKids1: The Saturn V was 111 m (363 ft) tall — about as tall as a 36-storey building, and 18 m (60 ft) taller than the Statue of Liberty.
lab.apolloFactKids2: Fully fuelled for launch, it weighed 2.8 million kg (6.2 million lb) — about as much as 400 elephants.
lab.apolloFactKids3: At launch it pushed with 7.6 million pounds of thrust — more power than 85 Hoover Dams.
lab.apolloFactKids4: It could carry about 118,000 kg to Earth orbit — about 10 school buses — or about 43,500 kg to the Moon, like four school buses.
lab.apolloFactKids5: The first Saturn V flew in 1967. The last, in 1973, launched the Skylab space station with only two stages and no crew.
lab.apolloFactKids6: Of the whole rocket, only the Command Module Columbia came back. It splashed down in the Pacific Ocean on 24 July 1969 with Neil Armstrong, Buzz Aldrin and Michael Collins.
lab.launchMissionMaxQHint: Switch the clock to 1x before T+01:23
lab.launchMissionStaging: See the first stage fall away
lab.launchExplainSimple: Getting into orbit is not mostly about going up — it is about going sideways, very fast. The rocket climbs straight up, then leans over and keeps speeding up. At about 7.8 km/s it falls towards Earth exactly as fast as Earth's surface curves away beneath it, so it never lands: that is an orbit.
lab.launchExplainFormula1: v(orbit) = √(GM / r) ≈ 7.8 km/s   at r = 6,371 + 188 km
lab.launchExplainFormula2: q = ½ · ρ · v²   (dynamic pressure — Max-Q is its peak)
lab.launchExplainDetails: On the way up the air density ρ falls while the speed v rises, so their product q peaks once — for Apollo 11 at T+1:23. The first stage burns kerosene with a bright orange flame; the second and third burn hydrogen, whose flame is almost invisible. Watch the speed bar during the third stage: the height barely changes, the speed is what grows.
lab.launchFact1: Apollo 11 lifted off at 9:32 in the morning, Florida time (13:32 UTC), on 16 July 1969, from Launch Complex 39A.
lab.launchFact2: Max-Q came at T+1:23: the moment the air pressed hardest on the rocket. After it the air thins out faster than the speed grows.
lab.launchFact3: The launch escape tower was thrown away at T+3:18, about 96 km up. From then on, other ways of aborting the flight took over.
lab.launchFact4: Apollo 11 entered Earth orbit at T+11:49, about 188 km up, moving at 7.79 km/s — about 28,000 km/h.
lab.launchFact5: At engine cutoff Michael Collins read the orbit out as "101.4 by 103.6" — nautical miles, about 188 and 192 km: very nearly a circle.
lab.launchFact6: The third stage hardly climbed: in its 150-second burn the altitude grew by about 2 km, but the speed by about 850 m/s.
lab.apolloQuizWhySic: The first stage was dropped at T+2:42 and fell into the Atlantic.
lab.apolloQuizWhySii: The second stage was dropped at T+9:09 and fell back into the Atlantic.
lab.apolloQuizWhySivb: The third stage sent the crew towards the Moon, then was steered into an orbit around the Sun.
lab.apolloQuizWhyLes: The escape tower was thrown away at T+3:18, long before the trip home.

lab.satExplainSimple: A satellite is falling towards the Earth all the time! But it flies sideways so fast that, as it falls, the curved ground drops away beneath it — so it never lands. Higher up, the Earth's pull is weaker, so the satellite moves more slowly and each lap takes longer.
lab.satExplainDetails: Orbits here are circles (eccentricity 0). The time in shadow uses a cylindrical shadow and the Sun's direction in the picture; in reality it changes through the year with the angle between the orbit and the Sun. For high orbits the view zooms out but keeps the Earth and the orbit to one scale; the spacecraft are enlarged so they can be seen.
lab.satFact1: The ISS goes around the Earth about every 90 minutes, so its crew sees about 16 sunrises and 16 sunsets every day.
lab.satFact2: The first artificial satellite, Sputnik 1, was launched on 4 October 1957. It took about 98 minutes to go once around the Earth.
lab.satFact3: GPS satellites fly about 20 200 km up and go around the Earth twice a day. At least 24 of them are in service, so at least four can be seen from almost anywhere on Earth.
lab.satFact4: In 1945 the writer and engineer Arthur C. Clarke proposed putting three relay satellites in geostationary orbit to connect the whole world by radio — twelve years before the first satellite flew.
lab.satFact4Source: A. C. Clarke, “Extra-Terrestrial Relays”, Wireless World, October 1945
lab.satFact5: From geostationary height a satellite sees about 42% of the Earth's surface — check it with the “Earth in view” readout. From the ISS you see only about 3%.
lab.satFact6: Geostationary satellites are in sunlight almost all the time. Only for a few weeks around the March and September equinoxes do they pass through the Earth's shadow — for up to about 70 minutes a day.
lab.satFact6Source: Orbital geometry, computed in this lab
lab.satFact7: Cosmonaut Vladimir Dzhanibekov, born in 1942 in the Tashkent region, flew to space five times. In 1985 he noticed a spinning wing nut flipping over every few seconds in weightlessness — physicists now call it the Dzhanibekov effect.
lab.satFact7Source: Gagarin Cosmonaut Training Center, cosmonaut biography
lab.falconSubtitle: A two-stage rocket whose first stage flies back and lands so it can be used again. Turn the model with the mouse; with the camera switched on you can also steer it with hand gestures.
lab.falconScale: 70 m is about a 23-storey building (≈3 m a floor). The Tashkent TV Tower (375 m) is more than five times taller.
lab.falconQ1: Why does the first stage of Falcon 9 come back and land?
lab.falconQ1a: To be used again — it makes flights cheaper
lab.falconQ1b: To bring the second stage back
lab.falconQ1c: To refuel and take off again within the hour
lab.falconQ1Right: Right! A rocket stage is very expensive; landing it means it can fly again. Some Falcon 9 first stages have flown more than 20 times.
lab.falconQ1Wrong: Not quite. The second stage goes on to orbit and does not come back; the first stage lands so it can be reused, which makes flights cheaper.
lab.falconQ2: What does the “9” in Falcon 9 stand for?
lab.falconQ2b: The nine Merlin engines of its first stage
lab.falconQ2Right: Right! Nine Merlin engines push the first stage; the second stage has one Merlin Vacuum engine.
lab.falconQ2Wrong: Not quite. The number counts the nine Merlin engines on the first stage.
lab.falconQ3: How does the first stage slow down to land?
lab.falconQ3b: It unfolds wings and glides like a plane
lab.falconQ3c: It restarts its engines to brake, steering with grid fins
lab.falconQ3Right: Right! It lands upright on its engine and four landing legs — on land, or on a ship at sea.
lab.falconQ3Wrong: Not quite. The booster has no parachute and no wings: it brakes with its own engines and steers with grid fins.
lab.falconMissionQuiz_landing: Answer: how it brakes to land
lab.falconExplainSimple: About two and a half minutes after lift-off the first stage separates. Instead of falling into the sea, it turns around, fires its engines again to slow down, steers through the air with four grid fins, unfolds its legs and lands standing upright — a bit like balancing a pencil on your fingertip.
lab.falconFormulaConstants: g₀ = 9.80665 m/s²; m₀ — mass with fuel, m₁ — mass after the burn
lab.falconExplainDetails: Tsiolkovsky's rocket equation: the speed a rocket can gain depends on how much of its mass is fuel. Fuel kept back for landing cannot be used to push the payload, so a reusable launch carries less than a throw-away one. Returning to the launch site needs a “boostback” burn first; a landing on a ship out at sea usually does not.
lab.falconFact1: The first Falcon 9 first stage to land came down on 21 December 2015, after launching 11 Orbcomm satellites.
lab.falconFact2: The first reflight of a landed first stage was on 30 March 2017, launching the SES-10 satellite.
lab.falconFact3: Some Falcon 9 first stages have now flown more than 20 times.
lab.falconFact4: The ships the boosters land on at sea are named after spaceships in Iain M. Banks's science-fiction novels — one is called “Of Course I Still Love You”.
lab.falconFact5: On 30 May 2020 a Falcon 9 launched NASA astronauts Bob Behnken and Doug Hurley to the ISS in a Crew Dragon — the first crewed flight to orbit of a commercially built spacecraft.
lab.falconFact6: The name comes from the Millennium Falcon spaceship in Star Wars and from the nine engines of the first stage.

lab.exoExplainSimple: Hold a coin in front of a torch and the light dims a little. A planet does the same to its star when it passes in front of it. The bigger the planet compared with the star, the deeper the dip — so a small planet is easier to spot in front of a small star. The time between two dips is the planet's year.
lab.exoExplainFormula3: a³ = G · M★ · P² / 4π²   (Kepler's third law)
lab.exoExplainDetails: ΔF is the fraction of light lost, Rp and R★ the radii of the planet and the star, P the time between dips. Astronomers measure ΔF and P from the light curve and take R★ from the star's spectrum, which gives the planet's size; Kepler's third law with the star's mass M★ gives the size of the orbit, a. How long a dip lasts depends on both: T ≈ (P / π) · arcsin(R★ / a).
lab.exoFact1: The first planet found round a Sun-like star, 51 Pegasi b, was discovered in 1995 by Michel Mayor and Didier Queloz — from the wobble it gives its star. They shared the 2019 Nobel Prize in Physics.
lab.exoFact2: HD 209458 b was the first planet ever seen passing in front of its star, in 1999 — the same planet as the first real example here.
lab.exoFactSrc2: Charbonneau et al. (2000), ApJ 529, L45; Henry et al. (2000), ApJ 529, L41
lab.exoFact3: The Kepler space telescope stared at one patch of sky from 2009 to 2018 and found more than 2 600 confirmed planets with this method.
lab.exoFact4: TESS, launched in April 2018, scans almost the whole sky strip by strip and watches each strip for about 27 days — which is why so many of its planets have short years.
lab.exoFact5: TRAPPIST-1, a star only a little bigger than Jupiter, has seven Earth-sized planets, all found by their transits.
lab.exoFact6: Seen from far away, Earth dims the Sun by just 0.008 % for about 13 hours, once a year. That is why Earth twins round Sun-like stars are so hard to find.
lab.exoFact7: HD 189733 b is deep blue — the Hubble telescope measured its colour in 2013. It is no ocean world, though: it is a scorching gas giant.
lab.hrStorySun: Our own star. Its light takes 8 minutes 20 seconds to reach us. In about 5 billion years it will swell into a red giant.
lab.hrStorySiriusA: The brightest star in the night sky. In Uzbekistan look south on winter evenings: follow the three stars of Orion's belt down and to the left.
lab.hrStoryBetelgeuse: Orion's red shoulder on winter evenings. It is so big that, put in the Sun's place, it would swallow the orbit of Mars. In 2019–2020 it dimmed for a while behind its own dust.
lab.hrStoryProxima: The nearest star after the Sun, 4.24 light-years away. It is too faint to see without a telescope, and from Uzbekistan it never rises at all — it is deep in the southern sky.
lab.hrStoryRigel: Orion's blue-white foot, one of the brightest stars of the winter sky. It gives out about a hundred thousand times more light than the Sun.
lab.hrStorySiriusB: Sirius's tiny companion, a white dwarf: about the size of Earth, but with nearly the mass of the Sun. A teaspoon of it would weigh more than ten tonnes.
lab.hrStoryArcturus: The brightest star in the northern half of the sky, an orange giant. On spring and summer evenings, follow the curve of the Big Dipper's handle and you arrive at it.
lab.hrStoryVega: The brightest star of the Summer Triangle. On summer evenings in Uzbekistan it shines almost straight overhead.
lab.hrStoryAldebaran: The orange eye of Taurus the Bull, a giant star of autumn and winter evenings.
lab.hrStoryProcyon: The bright star of the Little Dog. With Sirius and Betelgeuse it makes the Winter Triangle. It too has a white dwarf companion, Procyon B.
lab.hrStoryDeneb: The third star of the Summer Triangle. It is very far away and still easy to see — it gives out hundreds of thousands of times more light than the Sun.
lab.hrStoryEpsEri: A star a little smaller and much younger than the Sun, 10.5 light-years away, wrapped in a ring of dust. From a dark place you can see it without a telescope.
lab.hrStory40EriB: The easiest white dwarf to find with a small telescope. It belongs to a family of three stars: 40 Eridani A, B and C.
lab.hrQuizBiggest: Which of these stars is the biggest?
lab.hrQuizBiggestWhy: Right — Betelgeuse is about 760 times wider than the Sun. Put in the Sun's place, it would reach past the orbit of Mars.
lab.hrQuizHottest: Which of these stars is the hottest?
lab.hrQuizHottestWhy: Right — Sirius B's surface is about 25 000 K, more than four times hotter than the Sun's. Being so small, it is still faint.
lab.hrQuizNearest: Which of these stars is the nearest to us?
lab.hrQuizNearestWhy: Right — Proxima Centauri is 4.24 light-years away, the nearest star after the Sun. Its light takes more than four years to reach us.

lab.hrExplainSimple: Heat a piece of iron and it glows red, then yellow, then bluish-white. Stars do the same: their colour tells their temperature. How much light a star gives out depends on its temperature and its size — so a cool red star can still be dazzling if it is enormous, like Betelgeuse.
lab.hrExplainDetails: Both axes are logarithmic: each grid line is a factor of 100 in brightness. Temperature runs backwards, hot on the left, as astronomers have drawn it since Hertzsprung and Russell. From a star's temperature and brightness the first formula gives its radius; the second gives the colour it shines brightest in — the Sun peaks near 500 nm, in green-blue light.
lab.hrFact1: The diagram is named after Ejnar Hertzsprung of Denmark and Henry Norris Russell of the USA, who drew it independently in the 1910s.
lab.hrFact2: About nine stars in ten, the Sun among them, sit on the main sequence: they shine by turning hydrogen into helium in their cores.
lab.hrFact3: A star's colour is its thermometer: red stars are about 3 000 K, yellowish ones like the Sun about 6 000 K, and blue-white ones above 10 000 K.
lab.hrFact4: Betelgeuse's Great Dimming of 2019–2020 was caused by a cloud of dust the star itself had thrown out.
lab.hrFact5: Sirius B was first seen in 1862 by Alvan Graham Clark while he was testing a new telescope lens.
lab.hrFact6: In about 5 billion years the Sun will become a red giant, then shed its outer layers and end as a white dwarf about the size of Earth.
lab.hrFactSrc6: NASA Science, Our Sun; Sackmann, Boothroyd & Kraemer (1993)

lab.moonExplainSimple: Stand in a dark room with a lamp on one side and hold a ball at arm's length. Turn slowly on the spot: the lit half of the ball turns towards you or away from you, and you see a thin crescent, a half, then a full circle. The Moon is the ball, the Sun is the lamp, and you are standing on Earth.
lab.moonExplainFormula1: θ = 360° × age / 29.53 d   (the angle between the Moon and the Sun)
lab.moonExplainFormula3: synodic month (new to new) 29.53 d  ·  sidereal month (one turn among the stars) 27.32 d
lab.moonExplainDetails: The month of phases is about 2.2 days longer than one trip round Earth: meanwhile Earth moves about 27° along its orbit, and the Moon has to catch up with the Sun's direction. An eclipse also needs the Moon near a node — a point where its orbit, tilted 5.1°, crosses Earth's — at new or full moon.
lab.moonFact1: We always see the same face of the Moon: it spins once on its axis in exactly the time it takes to go once around Earth. This is called tidal locking.
lab.moonFact2: The Moon is drifting away from Earth by about 3.8 cm a year. Scientists measure this by bouncing laser light off mirrors that Apollo astronauts left on its surface.
lab.moonFact3: The Moon is about 384 400 km away on average. Light needs about 1.3 seconds to cross that gap, so we always see the Moon as it was 1.3 seconds ago.
lab.moonFact4: Total solar eclipses happen thanks to a coincidence: the Sun is about 400 times wider than the Moon but also about 400 times farther away, so both look almost the same size in our sky.
lab.moonFact5: Next to a thin crescent, the “dark” part of the Moon often glows faintly. This is earthshine — sunlight bounced off Earth onto the Moon. Leonardo da Vinci explained it about 500 years ago.
lab.moonFact6: Months of the Islamic (Hijri) calendar begin with the young crescent after new moon. Twelve lunar months last about 354 days, so Ramadan comes about 11 days earlier each year in the Gregorian calendar.
lab.moonFact7: Eclipses come in “seasons” about every 173 days — only when the Sun is near one of the two points where the Moon's tilted orbit crosses Earth's.
lab.moonFactSource7: NASA Eclipse Web Site (F. Espenak); J. Meeus, Astronomical Algorithms (1998)

lab.seasonExplainSimple: Shine a torch straight down at a table and you get a small, bright spot. Tilt the torch, and the same light spreads into a long oval, so every bit of the table gets less. In summer our half of Earth leans towards the Sun: its light comes in steeply and the day is long. In winter we lean away: the light comes in low, spreads out, and the day is short.
lab.seasonExplainFormula1: sin δ = sin ε · sin λ   (δ the Sun's declination, ε the axial tilt, λ the Sun's longitude)
lab.seasonExplainFormula3: cos H₀ = (sin(−0.833°) − sin φ · sin δ) / (cos φ · cos δ),   day = 2·H₀ / 15° hours
lab.seasonExplainFormula4: noon light on flat ground ∝ sin h
lab.seasonExplainDetails: λ comes from the US Naval Observatory's approximate solar coordinates. The −0.833° accounts for refraction and the Sun's radius — which is why even at the equinox the day is a few minutes longer than 12 hours. Sunrise and sunset clock times add the city's longitude, its time zone and the equation of time.
lab.seasonFactSource1: NASA Space Place — What causes the seasons?
lab.seasonFact2: Uranus is tilted about 98° — it rolls around the Sun on its side. Each of its poles gets about 42 years of daylight, then about 42 years of darkness.
lab.seasonFact3: Navruz is celebrated on 21 March, close to the March equinox, which falls on 19–21 March. On that day the Sun stands overhead at the equator, and day and night are almost equal all over Earth.
lab.seasonFactSource3: UNESCO — Nowruz, Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage
lab.seasonFact4: In Murmansk, the largest city north of the Arctic Circle, the Sun does not rise for about {days} days around the December solstice — and in June it does not set at all.
lab.seasonFactSource4: Encyclopaedia Britannica — Murmansk; days calculated in this lab
lab.seasonFact5: In Cape Town it is summer in December and winter in June: when the northern half of Earth leans away from the Sun, the southern half leans towards it. There the noon Sun is in the north.
lab.seasonFactSource5: NASA Space Place — What causes the seasons?
lab.seasonFact6: In Quito, almost on the equator, the day lasts about 12 hours all year: the longest and the shortest day differ by only about {minutes} min.
lab.seasonFactSource6: Calculated in this lab (US Naval Observatory formula)
lab.seasonFact7: Nukus lies almost 10° west of Tashkent, so by the same clock the Sun reaches its highest point there about {minutes} minutes later.
lab.seasonFactSource7: Calculated: 4 minutes of time per degree of longitude
lab.seasonFact8: Earth's tilt is not fixed: over about 41 000 years it slowly swings between about 22.1° and 24.5° — one of the Milankovitch cycles that shape the ice ages.

lab.biruniExplainMethod: Climb a mountain and the horizon drops a little below eye level, because the Earth curves away beneath you. A small ball curves sharply, a huge one gently — so that tiny angle, together with the mountain’s height, tells you how big the whole Earth is.
lab.biruniFormulaMethod2: R = h · cos α / (1 − cos α) ≈ 2h / α²
lab.biruniExplainMethodMore: In the short form α is in radians. Because R grows as 1/α², every 1 % of error in the angle becomes 2 % in the radius — which is why Biruni needed a fine instrument and a high place to stand. Light bending in the air (refraction) lifts the horizon slightly; this model leaves it out.
lab.biruniFactBorn: Abu Rayhan Biruni was born in 973 near Kath in Khwarazm — today Karakalpakstan, in Uzbekistan.
lab.biruniFactResult: His Earth radius, converted to kilometres, is about 6 340 km (6 339.6 km) — within half a per cent of today’s mean value, 6 371 km.
lab.biruniFactHorizon: From the top of Everest the horizon is about 336 km away; for a person standing on a beach it is only about 4.7 km.
lab.biruniFactHeight: Height helps: from the Tashkent TV Tower one arcminute of error changes the radius by about 5 %, from Everest by only about 1 %.
lab.biruniFactCrater: A crater on the far side of the Moon is named Al-Biruni in his honour; the name was adopted in 1970.

lab.biruniRulerTitle: Ruler under the shadow’s tip, magnified
lab.biruniRulerHint: The Sun is half a degree wide, so the edge is blurry: read its middle
lab.biruniExplainEra: The Sun is so far away that its rays arrive almost parallel. If a stick in one city casts no shadow at noon while a stick farther north does, the ground there must be tilted — because the Earth is round. That tilt is the same part of a full circle as the distance between the cities is of the whole way round.
lab.biruniExplainEraMore: With a 1 m stick and θ = 7.2° (one fiftieth of a circle) the shadow is 12.6 cm long. The Sun is about half a degree wide, so the shadow’s tip is blurred over almost a centimetre — read the middle. Eratosthenes assumed that Syene and Alexandria lie on one meridian and that the Sun stood exactly overhead in Syene; neither is quite true.
lab.biruniFactEratosthenes: Eratosthenes (about 276–194 BC) was the head of the great Library of Alexandria.
lab.biruniFactSyene: Syene is today’s Aswan, in the south of Egypt.
lab.biruniFactCleomedes: We know his method mainly from Cleomedes, who gives 5 000 stadia between the cities and 250 000 stadia around the Earth; other ancient writers quote 252 000.
lab.biruniFactStadion: Nobody knows exactly how long his stadion was. With 157.5 m his Earth comes out 1.6 % too small; with the Attic 185 m, about 16 % too big.
lab.biruniFactParallel: Sunlight arrives in almost parallel rays because the Sun is about 150 million km away — some 23 500 times the Earth’s radius.

lab.biruniExplainSextant: At noon the Sun stands as high as it will that day. In summer it climbs high, in winter it stays low. Halfway between the two lies the sky’s equator, which shows how far north you are; half the difference is how much the Earth’s axis is tilted.
lab.biruniExplainSextantMore: At noon the Sun’s height is h = 90° − latitude ± tilt. The model uses today’s tilt, 23.44°, and leaves out refraction, which lifts a low winter Sun by a few arcminutes.
lab.biruniFactUlughBeg: Ulugh Beg (1394–1449), a grandson of Amir Temur, ruled Samarkand and was one of the leading astronomers of his time.
lab.biruniFactObservatory: His observatory was built in Samarkand in the 1420s. Its giant meridian arc, the Fakhri sextant, had a radius of about 40 m.
lab.biruniFactVyatkin: The observatory was lost for centuries. In 1908 the archaeologist Vasily Vyatkin found it and dug out the underground part of the arc — you can still see it in Samarkand.
lab.biruniFactCatalogue: His star catalogue of 1437 gives the positions of about a thousand stars — 1 018 in the version most often quoted — most of them measured anew in Samarkand.
lab.biruniFactUlughBegNames: A crater on the Moon, Ulugh Beigh, and the asteroid 2439 Ulugbek are named after him.
lab.uniSubtitle: A star's mass decides how long it lives and how it dies. Pick a star and follow its whole life.
lab.uniOutlives: This star lives longer than the universe has existed so far (13.8 billion years) — no star like it has died yet.
lab.uniSunNow: The Sun is {age} old — about halfway through this stage.
lab.uniStageNebulaDesc: A huge cloud of gas and dust. Where part of it collapses under its own weight, a star is born.
lab.uniStageMainSequenceDesc: Hydrogen fuses into helium in the core. A star spends about 90 % of its life in this stage.
lab.uniStageRedGiantDesc: The core runs out of hydrogen and the star swells to around a hundred times its width, cooler and redder. When the Sun does this it is expected to swallow Mercury and Venus.
lab.uniStagePlanetaryNebulaDesc: The star puffs its outer layers into space as a glowing shell. Despite the name it has nothing to do with planets: in old telescopes these shells looked like planets' discs.
lab.uniStageWhiteDwarfDesc: What is left is the hot core: about a Sun's worth of matter squeezed into a ball the size of the Earth. It no longer burns and slowly cools for billions of years.
lab.uniStageHeliumWhiteDwarfDesc: A star this light burns for trillions of years and is expected to end as a white dwarf made of helium. The universe is still far too young: none has formed yet.
lab.uniStageRedSupergiantDesc: A heavy star swells into a red supergiant — Betelgeuse is one. Its core builds ever heavier elements, up to iron.
lab.uniStageSupernovaDesc: The iron core can no longer hold up its own weight: it collapses in an instant and the star explodes. For weeks it can outshine a whole galaxy.
lab.uniStageNeutronStarDesc: The collapsed core: a ball about 20 km across, heavier than the Sun. Many spin fast and sweep beams round like a lighthouse — we see them as pulsars.
lab.uniStageBlackHoleDesc: The core is so heavy that nothing — not even light — can escape. A disc of hot gas swirling around it glows brightly.
lab.uniToHr: See these stars on the H-R diagram
lab.uniMissionSunFuture: Follow a Sun-like star to its end: a white dwarf
lab.uniMissionSunFutureHint: Choose the Sun and go to the last stage
lab.uniMissionOutlive: Find a star that will outlive today's universe
lab.uniMissionOutliveHint: Its lifetime must be longer than 13.8 billion years
lab.uniMissionShortLife: Find a star that lives less than 10 million years
lab.uniMissionBlackHoleHint: Only the heaviest stars end this way
lab.uniExplainSimple: A star is a giant ball of gas. In its core, hydrogen fuses into helium and gives off energy. A heavy star has more fuel but burns it much, much faster — like a big truck that empties its tank sooner than a small car. That is why heavy stars live short lives and end in the biggest explosions.
lab.uniExplainFormula1: L ≈ M^3.5   (L and M in Sun units)
lab.uniExplainFormula2: t ≈ 10 billion years × M / L ≈ 10 billion years × M^-2.5
lab.uniExplainDetails: The panel's numbers come from a fit to detailed stellar models (Hurley, Pols & Tout 2000, solar composition), not from this simple rule. The rule gets the trend right but makes the heaviest stars die too young: a 30 M☉ star lives about 6 million years, not 2. The mass limits (about 8 and 20 M☉) are approximate — rotation, composition and a companion star matter too.
lab.uniFact1: The Sun is about 4.6 billion years old — roughly halfway through its life on the main sequence. In about 5 billion years it will swell into a red giant.
lab.uniFact2: A white dwarf packs about as much mass as the Sun into a ball roughly the size of the Earth.
lab.uniFact3: A neutron star is only about 20 km across — the size of a city — yet heavier than the Sun.
lab.uniFact4: In 1054 Chinese astronomers recorded a 'guest star' bright enough to see in daylight. Its remains are the Crab Nebula, with a pulsar at its heart spinning about 30 times a second.
lab.uniFact5: Supernova 1987A in the Large Magellanic Cloud was the closest supernova seen in almost 400 years, and the first whose neutrinos were caught on Earth.
lab.uniFact6: Betelgeuse, the red shoulder of Orion, is a red supergiant expected to explode as a supernova within the next 100,000 years.
lab.uniFact7: In 2019 the Event Horizon Telescope showed the first image of a black hole's shadow, in the galaxy M87; in 2022, the one at the centre of our own galaxy, Sagittarius A*.
lab.uniFact8: No red dwarf has ever died of old age: they live for trillions of years, and the universe is only 13.8 billion years old.
lab.uniModelNote: Pictures are not to scale: a red supergiant can be up to about a thousand times wider than the Sun, and a neutron star is 20 km across. Lifetimes are for the main-sequence stage (Hurley, Pols & Tout 2000); brightness from the mass–luminosity relation (Duric 2004); colours are approximate. Masses are at birth.
lab.planetSubtitle: Three worlds, three real processes — and the physics behind each one.
lab.planetGrainEnergy: A 1-gram grain at this speed carries about {kj} kJ — the energy of about {tnt} g of TNT. The air turns it into light and heat high above the clouds.
lab.planetTau: Dust in the air (optical depth τ)
lab.planetVent: Speed of gas from the vent
lab.planetGravityNote: Io pulls {value} times more weakly than the Earth and has almost no air, so the same throw goes {value} times higher. (The Earth figure ignores air resistance, which would make it far lower.)
lab.planetMissionNext: Find the next meteor shower on the calendar
lab.planetMissionStorm: Recreate the storm that silenced the Opportunity rover
lab.planetMissionPele: Build a plume as tall as Pele's (about 300 km)
lab.planetMissionPeleHint: Speed up the gas from the vent
lab.planetExplainEarth: Comets and some asteroids leave trails of dust along their orbits. Every year the Earth crosses the same trails on the same dates. The grains hit the air so fast that they heat it until it glows — a 'shooting star'. The faster the grain, the brighter it burns.
lab.planetDetailsEarth: ZHR is how many meteors one observer would see in an hour under a perfectly dark sky with the radiant overhead; real counts are usually lower. All meteors of one shower travel side by side, so they seem to fly out of one point in the sky — the radiant.
lab.planetExplainMars: Dust in the air blocks sunlight like a thick curtain over a window. Scientists measure how thick the curtain is with a number called the optical depth, τ. Each extra 1 in τ lets through only about a third as much of the direct sunbeam.
lab.planetDetailsMars: This is the direct beam (the Beer–Lambert law). Dust also scatters light around, so the sky never goes completely dark — but solar panels lose most of their power.
lab.planetExplainIo: Io has almost no air and its gravity is weak, so gas and lava thrown out of a volcano fly very high — like throwing a ball on a small moon instead of on Earth. Jupiter's gravity squeezes and stretches Io all the time, and that heats its insides.
lab.planetDetailsIo: g on Io = 1.796 m/s², on Earth 9.81 m/s². A simple throw with no air: real plumes are gas and dust that spread into umbrella shapes, but the heights match — Pele's vent speed of about 1 km/s gives about 300 km.
lab.planetFactEarth1: Every August the Earth crosses the dust of Comet Swift–Tuttle: that is the Perseids.
lab.planetFactEarth2: The Geminids come from an asteroid, 3200 Phaethon, not from a comet.
lab.planetFactEarth3: Halley's Comet gives us two showers a year: the Eta Aquariids in May and the Orionids in October.
lab.planetFactEarth4: In 1966 the Leonids turned into a meteor storm, with thousands of meteors a minute.
lab.planetFactEarth5: Most meteors burn up in the mesosphere, the layer of air about 50 to 85 km above the ground.
lab.planetFactEarth6: Meteors hit the air at between 11 and 72 km/s. The Leonids are among the fastest because they meet the Earth almost head-on.
lab.planetFactMars1: In June 2018 a dust storm wrapped the whole of Mars. The solar-powered Opportunity rover fell silent on 10 June 2018, after more than 14 years of work on a mission planned for 90 days.
lab.planetFactMars2: Mars' air is about 100 times thinner than Earth's, yet it can lift fine dust high enough to hide the whole planet.
lab.planetFactMars3: Global dust storms usually start in the southern spring and summer, when Mars is closest to the Sun.
lab.planetFactMars4: Dust devils — whirlwinds of dust — race across Mars, and gusts of wind have even cleaned dust off rovers' solar panels.
lab.planetFactMars5: Olympus Mons on Mars is the largest volcano in the Solar System.
lab.planetFactIo1: Io, a moon of Jupiter, is the most volcanically active world in the Solar System.
lab.planetFactIo3: In 2007 the New Horizons spacecraft photographed a plume 330 km tall above the volcano Tvashtar.
lab.planetFactIo4: Jupiter's pull flexes Io, and regular tugs from Europa and Ganymede keep its orbit slightly oval — so the squeezing never stops, and it heats Io from inside.
lab.planetFactIo5: Io has almost no impact craters: its volcanoes cover them up faster than new ones form.
lab.planetModelNote: Not to scale where it matters: the air is drawn thicker than its real ~100 km, Jupiter is drawn far smaller and closer than it is, and Io's map is a sketch of its colours, not a map of its surface. Io's plumes are drawn at true height. Shower data: International Meteor Organization and NASA; peak dates shift by about a day from year to year.
lab.planetScaleIo: Plumes at true height · Jupiter not to scale
lab.hzExtrapolated: {name} ({teff} K) is a little cooler than the 2600 K the zone formula was fitted for, so its zone is worked out at 2600 K — a small stretch of the model.
lab.hzPlanetsHint: A planet's dot turns orange, green or blue once you have visited it: too hot, in the zone, or too cold.
lab.hzWhyHot: Why too hot: it gets {flux} × the starlight Earth gets — enough to boil its oceans away in a runaway greenhouse, as probably happened to Venus.
lab.hzWhyLiquid: Why it could work: it gets {flux} × Earth's starlight — with a suitable atmosphere that is enough to keep water liquid.
lab.hzWhyCold: Why too cold: it gets only {flux} × Earth's starlight — even a thick carbon-dioxide atmosphere could not stop its water freezing.
lab.hzMissionZone: Put a planet in a habitable zone
lab.hzMissionBoil: Move a planet too close and boil its oceans
lab.hzMissionProxima: Visit Proxima b, around the nearest star to the Sun
lab.hzMissionProximaHint: Pick Proxima Centauri, then tap its planet.
lab.hzMissionTypes: Find the zone round all four kinds of star: M, K, G and F
lab.hzMissionTrappist: Find every TRAPPIST-1 planet that is in the zone
lab.hzMissionTrappistHint: Pick TRAPPIST-1 and tap its seven planets one by one.
lab.hzExplainSimple: It works like sitting by a campfire. Too close and you get scorched, too far and you shiver — somewhere in between it is just right. A small, dim star is a small campfire: you have to sit much closer to keep warm. That just-right ring is the habitable zone, where a planet like Earth could keep liquid water.
lab.hzExplainFormula1: Edge of the zone: d = √(L / S_eff)
lab.hzExplainDetails: d is in au, L is the star's brightness in Suns and A is the planet's albedo (0.3). Starlight falls as 1/d², so a star with 1/100 of the Sun's light has its zone 10 times closer. S_eff, the starlight at each edge, depends on the star's temperature (Kopparapu et al. 2013, 2014): inside the inner edge a runaway greenhouse boils the oceans; beyond the outer edge even thick CO₂ cannot keep water liquid.
lab.hzScaleNote: Distances to scale · star and planet sizes enlarged
lab.hzFact1: Proxima b circles Proxima Centauri, the closest star to the Sun, 4.2 light-years away — inside its star's habitable zone. A year there lasts just 11.2 days.
lab.hzFact2: TRAPPIST-1 has seven planets about the size of Earth, and three of them — e, f and g — are in its habitable zone. The whole system would fit inside Mercury's orbit.
lab.hzFact3: Being in the zone is not enough. Mars is inside the Sun's zone, but its air is less than 1% as thick as Earth's, so its water froze or escaped to space.
lab.hzFact4: Without its greenhouse effect Earth would average about −18 °C instead of +15 °C — a frozen world.
lab.hzFact5: Venus gets about twice Earth's sunlight and is the hottest planet in the Solar System: 464 °C at the surface, hotter than Mercury.
lab.hzFact6: Red dwarfs are the most common stars near the Sun — about three in every four — so many habitable zones hug small, dim stars.
lab.hzFactSource6: RECONS survey of nearby stars; NASA
lab.hzFact7: Kepler-452b orbits a Sun-like star once every 385 days, at almost Earth's distance. When it was found in 2015, NASA called it Earth's bigger, older cousin.

lab.uniMorphIgnite: Ignition: the core reaches about 10 million °C and hydrogen begins to fuse. A star is born.
lab.uniMorphSwell: The hydrogen in the core runs out. The core shrinks and heats up while the outer layers swell and cool.
lab.uniMorphDwarf: Over trillions of years the red dwarf uses up nearly all its hydrogen and shrinks into a white dwarf.
lab.uniMorphShed: The outer layers drift off into space and the hot core is laid bare.
lab.uniMorphFade: Within a few tens of thousands of years the shell spreads out and fades; the white dwarf is left.
lab.uniMorphCollapse: The iron core collapses in under a second; the rebound and a flood of neutrinos blow the star apart.
lab.uniMorphRemnant: The debris flies off, seeding space with new elements; the crushed core is left behind.
lab.uniNebulaCloud: A cold cloud of gas and dust, about −260 °C. Its densest clump starts to fall in under its own gravity.
lab.uniNebulaCollapse: The clump shrinks, and spins faster as it does — like a skater pulling in their arms — and flattens into a disc.
lab.uniNebulaProtostar: A protostar glows at the centre, heated by its own squeezing, not yet by fusion, and jets of gas shoot from its poles. The disc and jets here are DG Tau, a young star in Taurus, as NASA modelled it. For a star like the Sun, getting from here to fusion takes tens of millions of years.
lab.fusLayerConvectiveCore: Core — fusion, and the gas churns
lab.fusLayerRadiative: Radiative zone — light works its way out
lab.fusLayerConvective: Convective zone — hot gas rises, cool gas sinks
lab.fusCutawayNote: A quarter cut away. Energy is made only in the core, then travels out: as light staggering through the radiative zone, or carried by boiling gas in the convective zone.
lab.fusPp1Desc: Two protons collide hard enough to fuse. One turns into a neutron, giving off a positron and a neutrino; a proton and a neutron together are deuterium. This is the slow step: a proton in the Sun waits billions of years, on average, for its turn.
lab.fusPp2Desc: Within about a second the deuterium catches another proton and becomes helium-3, a light kind of helium. The spare energy leaves as a gamma ray.
lab.fusPp3Desc: Two helium-3 nuclei, each made by the first two steps, meet and become ordinary helium-4. Two protons are set free to fuse again.
lab.fusPpNetDesc: In all, four hydrogen nuclei become one helium nucleus. The helium weighs 0.7 % less than the four protons did: that missing mass is the energy, by E = mc², about 26.7 MeV each time.
lab.fusCno1Desc: A carbon nucleus captures a proton and becomes nitrogen-13.
lab.fusCno2Desc: Nitrogen-13 is unstable: within minutes one of its protons turns into a neutron, and it becomes carbon-13.
lab.fusCno3Desc: A second proton is captured: nitrogen-14.
lab.fusCno4Desc: A third proton: oxygen-15. This is the slowest step of the cycle.
lab.fusCno5Desc: Oxygen-15 decays in about two minutes into nitrogen-15.
lab.fusCno6Desc: The fourth proton splits the nucleus: out comes a helium-4, and the carbon-12 we started with is back.
lab.fusCnoNetDesc: The same result as the proton–proton chain, but carbon, nitrogen and oxygen do the work and come back unchanged: they are catalysts. The cycle needs a hotter core, so it powers stars heavier than about 1.3 Suns; in the Sun it makes only about 1 % of the energy.
lab.fusFact1: Every second the Sun fuses about 600 million tonnes of hydrogen into helium, and about 4 million tonnes of that mass becomes energy.
lab.fusFact2: The Sun's core is about 15 million °C. Light made there can take around 170 000 years to work its way out to the surface.
lab.fusFact3: About 65 billion neutrinos from the Sun's core pass through every square centimetre of you every second — at night too, straight through the Earth.
lab.fusFactSource3: J. N. Bahcall, solar neutrino flux
lab.fusSubtitle: Why do stars shine? Cut a star open, then step into its core and watch hydrogen become helium, nucleus by nucleus.
lab.fusMainHere: the main one in this star
lab.fusSunCounter: Since you opened this lab, the Sun has turned about {tonnes} tonnes of hydrogen into helium.
lab.fusMissionPp: Watch the proton–proton chain to the end
lab.fusMissionPpHint: Open “Reactions in the core” and let the chain run through
lab.fusMissionCno: See the carbon come back at the end of the CNO cycle
lab.fusMissionCnoHint: Choose the CNO cycle and watch all six steps
lab.fusMissionLayers: Compare a red dwarf's insides with a massive star's
lab.fusMissionLayersHint: Look at the star cut open for both presets
lab.fusExplainSimple: A star shines because its core is so hot and so squeezed that hydrogen nuclei crash into each other and stick, making helium. Helium weighs a tiny bit less than the hydrogen that made it, and that missing bit of mass turns into a huge amount of energy. The energy slowly works its way out and leaves the star as the light we see.
lab.fusExplainFormula2: E = Δm·c²,  Δm ≈ 0.7 % of the four protons' mass
lab.fusExplainDetails: Protons repel each other, and even at 15 million °C they almost never have enough energy to touch. They fuse anyway by quantum tunnelling, which is why the first step is so slow. The proton–proton chain speeds up roughly as T⁴ and the CNO cycle as about T¹⁶–T²⁰, so above a core temperature of about 17 million °C — stars heavier than about 1.3 Suns — the CNO cycle takes over. The animation shows the main branch of the proton–proton chain (pp-I); in the Sun two other branches, through beryllium and boron, also run.
lab.fusFact4: In 1920 Arthur Eddington suggested that the Sun shines by turning hydrogen into helium. In 1939 Hans Bethe worked out the reactions — both the proton–proton chain and the CNO cycle — and won the 1967 Nobel Prize for it.
lab.fusFact5: The Borexino detector under Italy's Gran Sasso mountain caught neutrinos from the proton–proton chain in 2014 and from the CNO cycle in 2020 — direct proof that both run in the Sun.
lab.fusFact6: On Earth, the National Ignition Facility first got more fusion energy out of a fuel capsule than its lasers put in on 5 December 2022: 3.15 MJ out for 2.05 MJ in.
lab.fusFact7: Fusion stops paying at iron: making nuclei heavier than iron takes energy instead of giving it. That is why a massive star's core ends as iron — and then collapses.
lab.fusModelNote: Not to scale: a nucleus is about 100 000 times smaller than an atom, and in a real core the nuclei move far faster and fuse far more rarely. The proton–proton chain shown is its main branch (pp-I). Layer boundaries are approximate: about 0.25 and 0.7 of the radius in the Sun; a star is fully convective below about 0.35 M☉ and has a convective core above about 1.3 M☉.
lab.uniToFusion: How does a star shine? Open the fusion lab
lab.uniNebulaPillars: The Pillars of Creation in the Eagle Nebula: columns of cold gas and dust about four light-years tall, slowly worn away by the light of hot young stars. New stars are forming inside them. Let's fly into the tip of one.
lab.uniSupernovaBlast: The blast: a shock wave tears outward at thousands of kilometres a second, and for a few weeks the dying star can outshine its whole galaxy.
lab.uniSupernovaRemnant: What is left: Cassiopeia A, the remnant of a star whose explosion we see as about 340 years old, 11 000 light-years away. NASA reconstructed its 3D shape from X-ray, infrared and optical data.
lab.uniPlanetaryHelix: The Helix Nebula, about 650 light-years away: the outer layers of a Sun-like star drifting off at about 30 km/s. Oxygen glows blue-green inside, hydrogen and nitrogen red further out. The white dwarf left behind sits at the centre.
lab.uniPulsarCrab: A young pulsar's wind: the ring and jets of the Crab Nebula, blown by a neutron star spinning 30 times a second, as Chandra sees them in X-rays.

history.subtitle: Explore humanity's journey from ancient stargazing to modern space exploration — tap any era to dive deeper.

era1.title: Ancient Astronomy
era1.summary: Egyptian, Babylonian, American, and Greek scholars laid the foundation for calendars, eclipse calculations, and early cosmic ideas.
era1.details:
3000–2000 BC | Ancient Egypt: Stars were observed, and the first 365-day calendar was created. Time and distance measurement developed with sundials (obelisks).

1000–500 BC | Babylonian civilization: Planetary maps were drawn, and 12 zodiac signs were formed. Predicting lunar and solar eclipses was established.

500–200 BC | Ancient American peoples: Maya and Inca ancestors accurately calculated the movements of the Sun and Venus and built stone observatories.

300–100 BC | Ancient Greece: The Earth's circumference was calculated almost accurately, and the early forms of the heliocentric idea emerged.

era2.title: Central Asian Golden Age
era2.summary: From al-Farghani and al-Khwarizmi to Ulugh Beg's Samarkand observatory — Central Asian scholars advanced mathematics, astronomy, and star-mapping to unprecedented precision.
era2.details:
IX century | Ahmad al-Farghani (Alfraganus): Born in the Ferghana Valley, he wrote one of the most influential astronomy textbooks of the medieval world, summarising Ptolemy for students across the Islamic world and medieval Europe.

IX century | Muhammad al-Khwarizmi: The Khwarazm-born mathematician gave the world the word 'algorithm' and pioneered algebra, creating astronomical tables used from Baghdad to Córdoba.

XI century | Abu Rayhan al-Biruni: A polymath from Khwarazm who accurately estimated the Earth's radius using trigonometry, and wrote encyclopaedic works on astronomy, geography, and chronology.

1424–1449 | Mirzo Ulugh Beg: Timurid prince and astronomer who built the Samarkand Observatory — one of the most advanced in the medieval world. His star catalogue (Zij-i Sultani) listed 1,018 stars with remarkable precision and was used by astronomers for centuries.

era3.title: Scientific Revolution & the Telescope
era3.summary: Scholars from Copernicus to Newton laid the foundation for modern astronomy through the telescope and laws of physics.
era3.details:
1500s | Nicolaus Copernicus: Developed a revolutionary heliocentric system where the Sun, not the Earth, is at the centre of the universe.

1608 | Hans Lippershey: A Dutch master invented the first historical telescope that brought distant objects closer.

1609 | Galileo Galilei: The first scientist to point a telescope at the universe. He discovered lunar craters and 4 satellites of Jupiter, confirming Copernicus's ideas.

1611 | Johannes Kepler: Discovered the basic laws of planetary motion and created a more accurate astronomical telescope.

1687 | Isaac Newton: Physically proved why planets move in a certain orbit through the law of universal gravitation.

era4.title: Space Race & First Steps
era4.summary: In the period from Sputnik to Apollo 11, humanity went into space and took the first step on the Moon.
era4.details:
1957 | "Sputnik-1" and Laika: The first artificial satellite in human history was launched into orbit. Soon after, a dog named Laika became the first living creature to fly into space.

April 12, 1961 | Yuri Gagarin: The first person to fly into space on the "Vostok-1" ship. This was a huge historical step for all of humanity.

1963 & 1965 | Valentina Tereshkova became the first woman in space. Alexei Leonov became the first person to perform a spacewalk (12 minutes).

July 20, 1969 | "Apollo-11": Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin set foot on the lunar surface for the first time. Armstrong said his famous phrase: "That's one small step for man, one giant leap for mankind."

era5.title: Conquering the Planets
era5.summary: From landings on Venus and Mars to Voyager, Shuttle, Mir, and Hubble — this period saw humanity reach beyond Earth orbit.
era5.details:
1970–1971 | "Venera-7" was the first spacecraft to land on Venus. A year later, "Mars-3" successfully landed on Mars.

1977 | "Voyager" mission: Voyager-1 and Voyager-2 were launched to explore the frontiers of space. They are currently the most distant human-made objects.

1981–1986 | The reusable Space Shuttle made its first flight. The permanent modular station "Mir" was launched for long-term research.

1990–1997 | The Hubble telescope was launched into orbit, fundamentally changing our view of space. The complex Cassini-Huygens mission was sent to study Saturn.

era6.title: International Cooperation & Commercial Space
era6.summary: ISS, private rockets, Mars and Pluto missions, and the first image of a black hole took this era to a new level.
era6.details:
2000 | International Space Station (ISS): Permanent human living and working in space began with the first crew.

2008 | SpaceX successfully launched Falcon 1 — the first private spacecraft to reach orbit, starting the era of commercial space flights.

2012–2015 | Curiosity landed on Mars. New Horizons sent the first clear images of Pluto. A spacecraft landed on a comet (67P) for the first time.

2019 | The first actual photograph of a black hole (in galaxy M87) was captured, once again confirming Einstein's theory of relativity.

era7.title: New Horizons & Uzbekistan's Space Future
era7.summary: With James Webb, DART, Starship, and Uzbekistan's Samarkand-2028 satellite — humanity is actively entering the Moon, Mars, and a new era of national space programmes.
era7.details:
2021–2022 | The James Webb Space Telescope was launched to study the universe's oldest galaxies. The DART mission struck an asteroid to test planetary defence.

2023–2024 | India's Chandrayaan-3 landed on the Moon's south pole. SpaceX began Starship tests — the largest rocket ever built.

2026 | Uzbekistan launched the Samarkand-2028 hyperspectral satellite — the nation's first satellite in orbit. Artemis II astronauts orbited the Moon after a half-century break.

2028 | Uzbekistan prepares to launch the 'Mirzo Ulugbek' scientific CubeSat, host the IAC 2028 in Samarkand, and aims to send the first Uzbek cosmonaut into space.
